title: How to build a capacity planning model for AI support | Pylon
summary: Most capacity planning still assumes every ticket needs a human. See how AI agents change the math and how to plan headcount across agents and people.
body_markdown:
Agentic AI has changed the B2B customer support field, but many capacity planning strategies are still playing catch-up.
Capacity planning models often assume that every support ticket needs a person from end to end. Many teams are now running AI agents, which changes the equation.[Gartner predicts](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-03-05-gartner-predicts-agentic-ai-will-autonomously-resolve-80-percent-of-common-customer-service-issues-without-human-intervention-by-20290) that agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human intervention by 2029, leading to a 30% reduction in operational costs.


In this guide, we’ll explore how to create a capacity plan for a B2B support team that has adopted agentic AI. We’ll cover traditional lag, lead, and match strategies, and show you how to update them for a blended support model that handles volume spikes without shifting service quality.


## What capacity planning means for growing teams


Teams recurring assignments view from Pylon


[Scaling support teams](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/scaling-customer-support) need to have enough team members with the right skills ready to resolve higher ticket volumes. That’s what a capacity plan is for: Support leaders use historical ticket data to predict the expected workload and see if they have enough team members to cover it all. Then, they adjust staffing levels and tooling to plug any gaps.


Capacity planning is similar to resource planning, but differs in goals and timescale. Capacity planning focuses on creating a long-term strategy to help you meet customer demand. Resource planning puts team members and tools in place short-term, like building a weekly schedule.


After you have a capacity plan and allocated resources accordingly, you’ll need to keep tracking ticket volumes. Then, adjust staffing and team allocation when actual demand differs from what you forecasted for long-term capacity management.


## Common capacity planning models


These are the main types of capacity planning in operations management.


### Lag strategy


The lag strategy is reactive: When you see volumes increase, you increase team capacity to have the availability you need to meet the higher demand. It’s[cost efficient](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/improve-support-team-efficiency) because you only scale the team when you have proof of demand.


This strategy also introduces some risk. If you don’t respond quickly enough to volume spikes, response times slow. Late replies and breached[service level agreements (SLAs)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/service-level-agreements-pylon-guide) can threaten customer satisfaction while your team burns out.


### Lead strategy


The lead strategy is more proactive than lag. You increase hiring levels before higher volumes start. This is a good approach for fast-growing companies because it puts the resources in place to handle increasing ticket volume as it becomes a new normal. However, if the forecasted demand doesn’t happen, you’ll end up with excess capacity that can strain your budget.


### Match strategy


The match method aims to balance lead and lag strategies. You add capacity in anticipation of higher demand, but more often and in smaller amounts, so there’s less risk of excess capacity.


### Blended support model


The three traditional capacity planning strategies are based on[human teams](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/building-a-customer-support-team) handling each ticket, but many B2B support teams now work with AI agents. Today’s blended capacity planning models need to calculate manual and[automated capacity](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-support-automation) separately before unifying them into a single schedule.


## Common capacity planning challenges


Here are some common constraints that can prevent support teams from building accurate capacity models:


- **Inaccurate or incomplete historical data.** If your team answers customer questions on multiple channels, like Slack or live chat, without recording all that work in the same place, then you won’t be able to predict volumes accurately. (An[omnichannel approach](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/omnichannel-customer-support-definition-examples-strategy) can make this calculation easier.)
- **Ignoring shrinkage and occupancy.** Team members can’t work on tickets for 100% of their working hours. They also take breaks, have meetings, and do admin work. You need to account for this routine shrinkage in your capacity planning.
- **Treating ticket volume as uniform.** When you predict future volume based on all of your historical data, you might flatten volume spikes and seasonal swings into your average. Some tickets are also much more complex than others, so considering the overall workload is just as important as ticket volume.
- **Not accounting for AI in the staffing model.**[AI-powered customer service tools](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/ai-customer-service) save time for teams, but not considering how much AI agents can do means you may end up overstaffed. (We’ll cover more on this topic later.)
- **Reactive escalation patterns.** When teams don’t have consistent escalation rules and workflows, escalations and handoffs can create bottlenecks that add significantly to the workload for each ticket.


## How AI agents change capacity planning assumptions


Agent runbook view from Pylon


In a blended support model, capacity planning needs to look at more than just headcount. AI agents can resolve many issues autonomously and give customers instant answers to simple questions. They can also make support teams more efficient by investigating issues as they come in and suggesting solutions.


When predicting future demand, you’ll need to estimate how many tickets will be fully automated, AI-assisted, and human-only, and then calculate the workload accordingly.

The model uses actual agent resolution, escalation, and intervention rates to predict future capacity needs. As AI agents take on different amounts of the work, the tool updates the forecast workload for your team members.


When Pylon adopted an[Agentic Support model](https://www.usepylon.com/ebooks/how-pylon-adopted-agentic-support) , we saw a 72% improvement in first response time (FRT), which allowed us to revise our year-end hiring plan from 18 to 11 people while keeping the same growth forecast. The adoption also reduced our escalation workload. “Everyone's technical floor has risen,” says Pylon’s Support Engineering Manager Jon Clark. “Issues that once required two or three escalation steps can now be handled by nearly everyone on the team.”


## How to build a capacity plan in 6 steps


A capacity plan isn’t a one-time exercise. You’ll need to repeat it as your team grows and volumes change. Here are six steps for capacity planning you can follow every time.


### 1. Pull historical ticket volume and identify trends


Gather six to 12 months of ticket volume data from your analytics dashboard, broken out by channel and ticket type. Look for seasonal spikes and one-time events like contract renewals, product launches, and major outages, and separate them from the rest of the data so that they don’t distort average forecasts.


### 2. Measure handle time by ticket type


Find the average handle time (AHT) for different types of customer queries, and the difference in AHT between AI-assisted and human-only resolutions. This will help you create a more accurate forecast based on expected workload, not just ticket volume.


### 3. Establish your AI containment rate by segment


Calculate the containment rate for each ticket type. This is the percentage of tickets that are fully resolved by AI without team intervention or escalation. You’ll probably discover that simple issues and frequent questions have high containment rates, while more complex issues have low containment rates. Before adopting Agentic Support, Pylon’s AI agent was already autonomously resolving simple, routine questions, which made up around half of incoming tickets.


### 4. Calculate your human queue separately


Find the number of tickets your team will work on by subtracting AI-only tickets from the total number of incoming queries. Remember that these AI-assisted and team member-only issues tend to be more complex, so use your AHT data to forecast the workload for each type of ticket.


### 5. Apply shrinkage and occupancy targets


Calculate the amount of time your team spends on training, meetings, admin tasks, and anything else that’s not directly related to resolving customer issues. Then increase your capacity forecasts to account for that time.


For example, if your team will have 100 hours of work but a shrinkage rate of 20%, then you’ll need 125 hours of capacity. Keep in mind that AI agents don’t have shrinkage, so only apply this adjustment to the AI-assisted and team member-only ticket queue.


### 7. Build in a review cadence


Schedule regular reviews to check on and adjust your capacity plan. You’ll need to revisit your predictions at least every quarter, but plan to review more often if your AI containment rate shifts, if there’s a major product launch, or if your company is growing quickly and onboarding many new customers.

## FAQ


### What’s the best tool for capacity planning?


It depends on your customers, growth plan, and support team’s current workflows.[Pylon Workforce Management](https://www.usepylon.com/workforce-management) is built for blended support teams. It forecasts demand across AI agents and people, so B2B teams with complex, scaling enterprise relationships can plan coverage and headcount.


### What are the main challenges of using AI for capacity planning?


Some of the most common problems include insufficient historical data and false precision, where the AI model produces precise-looking predictions that aren’t based on your company’s actual numbers. Not accounting for ticket complexity (or AI agent’s ability) can also make capacity planning less accurate.


### What’s the difference between capacity planning and workforce management?


Capacity planning is the long-term strategic process for determining how much coverage and headcount you’ll need. Workforce management often encompasses day-to-day scheduling and utilization plus the scenario forecasting for capacity planning.
